extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining means-plus-function and step-plus-function claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), including tests to determine invocation of §112(f), disclosure requirements, and special considerations for computer-implemented claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong analysis for § 112(f) invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are instructed to use a three-prong test to determine if a claim limitation invokes § 112(f): (1) the use of “means,” “step,” or a generic placeholder; (2) functional language associated with these terms; and (3) absence of sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three prongs must be considered when deciding whether §112(f) applies. The memorandum reiterates that this three-prong framework governs interpretation of means-plus-function and step-plus-function limitations. Clear recordation of the examiner's application of this test is important for prosecution and later challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from use of 'means', 'step', or generic placeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The memo clarifies existing presumptions about the use of terms like “means” or “step” (or generic placeholders) in claims and their implications under §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of those words raises a presumption that §112(f) applies. That presumption can be overcome only by examining claim language and the common understanding in the relevant technological field (e.g., showing sufficient structure is recited). Examiners should carefully assess and record whether the presumption is rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional language associated with claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation uses functional language describing what the element does rather than reciting structure, material, or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether language is functional should be evaluated in context. Functional recitation combined with means/step or generic placeholders supports invoking §112(f). The examiner should note how the functional language contributes to the determination and whether supporting disclosure supplies structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of sufficient structure, material, or acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A key prong is that the claim does not recite sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim itself recites sufficient structure (or equivalent concrete material/acts), §112(f) may not be invoked despite functional language or use of ‘means/step.’ Examiners must evaluate claim text and common knowledge in the art to determine sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of supporting disclosure under §§ 112(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a §112(f) limitation, the adequacy of supporting disclosure must be evaluated under §§ 112(a) and (b), including assessment for definiteness, written description, and enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When §112(f) applies, examiners must assess whether the specification provides the requisite structure, acts, or materials to support the claimed function and whether the disclosure satisfies definiteness, written description, and enablement requirements. Deficiencies in the specification can render the limitation indefinite or unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear linkage between functional claim language and disclosed structure/material/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the necessity of clear linkage between the claim’s functional language and the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification to support the claimed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drafters should ensure the specification ties functional claim elements to corresponding structure or algorithms (as applicable). Examiners should look for explicit connection in the specification; absent a clear linkage, the claim may be vulnerable under written description/enablement/definiteness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for algorithm disclosure in computer-implemented claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-implemented claims under §112(f) must disclose a specific algorithm for the claimed function to meet definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms — mathematical formula, prose, a flowchart, or other manner — so long as it provides sufficient structure. Drafters should include sufficiently specific algorithms; examiners will look for algorithmic disclosure to avoid indefiniteness in functional computer-implemented claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner responsibility to record interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are reinforced in their role to make the record clear regarding their interpretation of §112(f) limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear documentation of why §112(f) is or is not invoked, what evidence rebuts or supports presumptions, and how disclosure was assessed is crucial for prosecution histories and any subsequent legal challenges. Examiners should explain determinations on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic drafting considerations for means-/step-plus-function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding means-plus-function and step-plus-function claim limitations can provide strategic advantages but requires careful framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be attentive to how such limitations are drafted because they may affect claim scope and enforceability. Drafting may intentionally invoke or avoid §112(f) consequences; the specification should be prepared to supply adequate structure/algorithms if functional language is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of narrower interpretation affecting patentability and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: §112(f) limitations may lead to a narrower interpretation of claims, influencing patentability and infringement analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because means/step limitations are limited to the structure/acts/materials disclosed and equivalents, claim scope can be narrower than comparable structural claim language. Applicants and practitioners should weigh this potential narrowing when deciding whether to use functional claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of describing claim elements as means/step without explicit supporting structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The memorandum notes that claim drafters may describe an element in a claim as a means or step for performing a specified function without explicitly stating the supporting structure, material, or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While permissible, doing so triggers the need for adequate supporting disclosure in the specification and careful consideration of the §112(f) consequences (see requirements for disclosure, algorithms for computer-implemented claims, and potential narrowing). Practitioners should ensure the specification supplies what will be required upon examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain awareness of USPTO resources and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The memorandum reminds examiners and practitioners of resources available for examining claims under §112(f) and clarifies that it reinforces existing practices rather than introducing new legal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should stay informed about USPTO guidance and updates to ensure consistent prosecution strategy. Use USPTO resources and precedents when evaluating or drafting functional claim limitations.
